sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Rewrite a blunt instruction as a polite suggestion suitable for a senior colleague.
items: Wir regen an, den Vorschlag erneut zu prüfen.
sections.lede: Say each line aloud once. This section is not scored.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: These are the three things you will be able to do by the end of the lesson.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Diplomatic German softens the demand without making the message vague.

blocks.text: High-stakes professional communication needs to be both clear and face-saving. German offers a range of tools: the subjunctive (“würden”, “könnten”), impersonal constructions (“es wäre hilfreich, wenn …”), and proposals framed as questions (“Wäre es denkbar, dass …?”).
Soften the form, not the content. “Wir regen an, den Vorschlag erneut zu prüfen” is polite but unambiguous. Pair every suggestion with a reason and a next step so the reader knows what to do.

blocks.title: Formality follows hierarchy and culture
blocks.text: Use “Sie” and full titles with senior external partners. In an established internal team, “du” with a softened request may be more natural. Match the register you hear around you.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

rows: Wir regen an, den Vorschlag erneut zu prüfen.
Wir würden uns über eine Rückmeldung freuen.
Wir bitten um Ihre Zustimmung zu dem Entwurf.

items: “Anregen” is more formal than “vorschlagen” and common in official letters.
“Erwägen” means to consider seriously; it takes an accusative object or a zu-infinitive.
“Bitten um” takes the accusative: um Ihre Zustimmung.

sections.title: Pronunciation

items.hint: The ä is long and open: er-VEH-gen.

blocks.text: German business letters often combine directness with formal courtesy. A sentence such as “Wir regen an, …” is both polite and clear; it does not need extra softening.
Hierarchy still shapes register. With senior partners, use titles and full forms; with peers, a shorter, warmer tone is acceptable.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Diplomatic structures
sections.lede: Soften the form while keeping the message precise.

blocks.text: The subjunctive “würden” and modal “könnten” lower the pressure of a request: Könnten Sie uns bis Freitag eine Rückmeldung geben?

sections.tip: Add a reason to every polite request. “Wir bitten um Zustimmung, weil die Frist naht” is easier to answer than a bare request.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Write and say a diplomatic message: a suggestion, a reason and a request for approval.

model.de: Wir regen an, den Zeitplan um eine Woche zu verlängern. Die Tests brauchen mehr Zeit, als geplant war. Wir bitten um Ihre Zustimmung zu dem angepassten Entwurf und würden uns über eine Rückmeldung freuen.
model.en: We suggest extending the schedule by one week. The tests need more time than planned. We request your approval of the revised draft and would be glad to receive a response.

tips: Use “Wir regen an, … zu …” for a formal suggestion.
Give a concrete reason before the request.
Close with a polite request for feedback.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.wrong: Wir regen an, den Vorschlag erneut prüfen.
items.right: Wir regen an, den Vorschlag erneut zu prüfen.
items.why: The infinitive clause needs zu before the verb.
The verb pattern is bitten um, not bitten für.

items.wrong: Wir würden uns über eine Rückmeldung freuen würden.
items.right: Wir würden uns über eine Rückmeldung freuen.
items.why: Würden appears once, before the infinitive.
